extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry; researchers learning the foundations of curves and elliptic curves
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and structural results about algebraic curves (especially genus 1), line bundles of various degrees, canonical embeddings, moduli heuristics, and the algebraic/group structure of elliptic curves. Includes explicit descriptions (Weierstrass form, j-invariant), geometric constructions (chords/tangents), and related exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of moduli space Mg
rubrics_metrics.description: For g > 1, dim Mg = 3g − 3 (Riemann). Genus 0 and 1 are exceptional (heuristics and examples show dim M0 = 0, dim M1 = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains heuristics for low g (counts from canonical embeddings / parameters), and remarks that stack/orbifold language accounts for automorphism groups (dimensions for moduli spaces can be adjusted accordingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment by automorphism groups: dim Mg − dim Aut Cg = 3g − 3
rubrics_metrics.description: For all g ≥ 0, dim Mg − dim Aut Cg = 3g − 3, where Aut Cg denotes the automorphism group of a curve of genus g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives data: regular curves of genus >1 have finite (0-dim) automorphism groups; genus 1 curves have 1-dimensional automorphism groups; genus 0 curves have 3-dimensional automorphism groups. In stack language, moduli dimensions reflect these automorphisms (e.g., moduli space dimension of genus 0 is −3, genus 1 is 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical curves are complete intersections up to low genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Curves of genus 3 through 5 can be understood as canonical curves realized as complete intersections; this approach fails for higher genus (exercise: show canonical curve of sufficiently large genus is not a complete intersection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides heuristics using canonical embeddings and references to Bézout’s theorem and earlier exercises. Explicitly warns that for g ≥ 6 the canonical model is not a complete intersection (Exercise 19.8.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of elliptic curve (as genus 1 with chosen point)
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic curve is a genus 1 curve E together with a choice of k-valued point p; the marked point is part of the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that a genus 1 curve without a chosen k-point is not called an elliptic curve; over some fields a genus 1 curve may have no k-valued points at all (examples over Q, R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical properties of genus 1 (differentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a genus 1 curve C, deg ωC = 2g − 2 = 0 and h0(C, ωC) = g = 1; the only degree 0 invertible sheaf with a section is OC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to the dualizing sheaf and uses Riemann-Roch / Serre duality to compute dimensions of spaces of sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch on genus 1 for positive degree line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L > 0 on a genus 1 curve, then h0(C, L) = deg L (since deg L − g + 1 = deg L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deduce embeddings and maps given by complete linear series for small degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 1 line bundles correspond to degree 1 points
rubrics_metrics.description: Each degree 1 (k-valued) point q determines a line bundle O(q), and conversely any degree 1 line bundle is O(q); distinct points give distinct line bundles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yields a canonical bijection (over algebraically closed fields) between degree 1 line bundles and closed points; twisting by O(−p) identifies degree 1 bundles with degree 0 invertible sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pic0 and group law on degree 1 points (Proposition 19.9.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree 0 invertible sheaves (under tensor product) form an abelian group; via the bijection this defines an abelian group structure on the degree 1 points of an elliptic curve with p as the identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially presented as a bijection of sets; the subsequent material shows this group law is algebraic (coming from a group variety structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mordell–Weil theorem (statement/exercise remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any elliptic curve E over Q, the Q-points E(Q) form a finitely generated abelian group (torsion part plus a free Z-module of finite rank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as context (classification of finitely generated abelian groups) and motivates the concept of Mordell–Weil rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 2 description: double cover of P1 branched at four points
rubrics_metrics.description: OE(2p) has 2 sections, giving E a degree-2 map to P1; in char ≠ 2 and over algebraically closed fields, this double cover is branched at four points (one of which is p), and conversely four distinct branch points determine the double cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to a parametrization of elliptic curves by branch points on P1, and explains the relation to level-2 structure (ordering the remaining three branch points). Use Riemann–Hurwitz and Proposition 19.5.2 for uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio and λ invariant for 4 branch points
rubrics_metrics.description: Given four ordered distinct points on P1 one can send three to (∞,0,1) and record the image λ of the fourth; λ ∈ P1 \\{0,1,∞} is the cross-ratio and classifies ordered 4-tuples up to Aut P1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permuting the three unmarked branch points yields six S3-related values of λ (λ, 1/λ, 1−λ, 1/(1−λ), (λ−1)/λ, λ/(λ−1)), so λ is a six-valued invariant of the unordered elliptic curve; motivates looking for an S3-invariant function j(λ).

rubrics_metrics.name: j-invariant classifies genus 1 curves (over algebraically closed fields, char ≠ 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a single algebraic invariant j such that j(λ) = j(λ′) iff λ and λ′ are related by the S3-actions above; genus 1 curves (not requiring a chosen point) over algebraically closed fields of characteristic ≠ 2 are classified up to isomorphism by the j-invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the classical formula j = 2^8 (λ^2 − λ + 1)^3 / (λ^2 (λ − 1)^2) (and remarks about the 2-power factors arising from characteristic 2 issues). Also remarks about the 6-to-1 cover P1_λ → P1_j and the q-expansion perspective on j.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 3: embedding via |O(3p)| and Weierstrass normal form
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete linear series |O(3p)| has h0 = 3 and gives a closed embedding E → P2 as a cubic curve; after coordinate changes (if char k ≠ 2,3) one can put the cubic into Weierstrass form y^2 z = x^3 + a x z^2 + b z^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains choice of coordinates placing p at [0,1,0] and making the line at infinity the flex line; notes where characteristic 2 or 3 obstructs simplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection from the marked point relates cubic model to the double cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Projecting the cubic from p to P1 (vertical projection [x,y,z] ↦ [x,z]) recovers the hyperelliptic double-cover description coming from |O(2p)|; sections x and z vanish to orders 1 and 3 respectively at p and generate O(2p) after twisting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains geometrically how the cubic model encodes the degree-2 map and how the linear series interplay produces the morphism to P1.

rubrics_metrics.name: j as function of Weierstrass coefficients (a,b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Weierstrass equation y^2 z = x^3 + a x z^2 + b z^3, the j-invariant can be computed as j(a,b) = 6912 a^3/(4 a^3 + 27 b^2) (classical formula up to normalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a direct link between the cubic (Weierstrass) coefficients and the moduli invariant; used to compare cubic and branch-point descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric group law via chords and tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: On the cubic model with origin p at infinity, if a line meets E at p1, p2, p3 then p1 + p2 + p3 = 0 in the group law; to add q and r intersect the line qr with E to get third point s and set q + r = −s (inverse obtained by connecting s to p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classical chord-and-tangent description gives the group law concretely; associativity is not immediate from geometry but follows from identification with Pic0 and the algebraicity of maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 4 embedding: complete intersection of two quadrics in P3
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete linear series |O(4p)| embeds E in P3 as the complete intersection of two quadrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: show the image lies in at least two independent quadrics, rule out reducible quadrics/components using Bézout and related exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-degree embeddings (degree 5 and beyond)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree-5 embedding is not a hypersurface complete intersection; rather it can be realized as the intersection of the Plücker-embedded G(2,5) with five hyperplanes (equations given by 4×4 Pfaffians of a 5×5 skew-symmetric matrix of linear forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates the geometric complexity increases with degree and that classical determinantal/Pfaffian descriptions appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraicity of inverse map (Proposition 19.10.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If char k ≠ 2,3, the map sending a degree-1 point to its inverse in the group law is a morphism of k-varieties (realized as the hyperelliptic involution y ↦ −y in Weierstrass coordinates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a warm-up to show group operations are algebraic, i.e., come from morphisms rather than mere set maps; the argument adapts in other characteristics with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of morphism t: (Creg × Creg) → Creg giving third intersection point
rubrics_metrics.description: For a geometrically integral cubic curve C ⊂ P2 (no lines), there is a unique morphism t on regular points such that t(p,q) is the third residual point of intersection of the line pq with C (and t(p,p) is where the tangent at p meets C). This construction commutes with base extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by local coordinates: write line PQ as x2 = m x1 + b, substitute into cubic to get a cubic in x1 whose third root is rational function −B/A − P1 − Q1; address exceptional loci by varying affine charts and glueing. Remarks about the small-field case (F2) and exercises on descent/field-of-definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic curves are group varieties (Theorem 19.10.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an elliptic curve (E,p) embedded by |O(3p)|, define e: Spec k → E (identity), i: E → E (inverse) via t, and m: E × E → E by (q,r) ↦ t(p,t(q,r)); then (E,e,i,m) satisfies the group axioms and is a group variety over k. These morphisms commute with arbitrary base extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument reduces to checking equalities on k-points over algebraically closed fields (identification with Pic0) and then uses that morphisms equal after base change must be equal originally; avoids writing down an explicit algebraic formula for addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard intuition: Pic0(E) wants to be a scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: The group law on degree-1 points stems from Pic0(E) (degree-0 invertible sheaves), and the algebraicity of the group operations suggests Pic0 should be representable by a scheme (the Picard scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions references for constructing moduli/ Picard varieties and that the group-variety structure on E realizes Pic0 in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degenerate elliptic curves realize classical algebraic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain degenerate genus-1 cubics (e.g., y^2 z = x^3 + x^2 z with marked p) lead to group-variety structures isomorphic to Gm (multiplicative group) or A1 (additive group) after removing a singular point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to produce isomorphisms of schemes and verify the group laws agree under these identifications, illustrating degenerations of elliptic curves to familiar algebraic groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poncelet’s Porism and elliptic-curve methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two nested ellipses in R^2 and the construction of successive tangent intersections, if the sequence of intersection points starting at some p0 is periodic (p0 = pn), then it is periodic for any starting point on the outer ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states the classical porism and notes that while elementary proofs exist, elliptic-curve techniques give a beautiful proof and connections to more advanced ideas (exercises explore the algebraic underpinnings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration morphism Fn periodicity property (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Fn be the nth iterate of the morphism t (defined as in Proposition 19.10.3). If Fn(p) = p for some closed point p, then Fn(x) = x for all x ∈ E (i.e., Fn is the identity on E), and n is a positive integer. Variations: show Fn is identity morphism under further hypotheses or over non-algebraically-closed fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise encourages strengthening the result and exploring field-of-definition issues; connects to Poncelet’s Porism via iterated maps on elliptic curves.
